question:
Your company has an Azure subscription that includes two virtual machines, named VirMac1 and VirMac2, which both have a status of Stopped (Deallocated).
The virtual machines belong to different resource groups, named ResGroup1 and ResGroup2.
You have also created two Azure policies that are both configured with the virtualMachines resource type. The policy configured for ResGroup1 has a policy definition of Not allowed resource types, while the policy configured for ResGroup2 has a policy definition of Allowed resource types.
You then create a Read-only resource lock on VirMac1, as well as a Read-only resource lock on ResGroup2.
Which of the following is TRUE with regards to the scenario? (Choose all that apply.)
options: A. You will be able to start VirMac1.
B. You will NOT be able to start VirMac1.
C. You will be able to create a virtual machine in ResGroup2.
D. You will NOT be able to create a virtual machine in ResGroup2.
explanation:
VirMac1 and the Read-only Lock:
A Read-only lock on a resource prevents any modifications or deletions to that resource.
Starting a virtual machine involves updating its state from Stopped (Deallocated) to Running, which is considered a write operation.
Because the lock prevents write operations, you will NOT be able to start VirMac1. This makes option B true and option A false.
ResGroup2 and the Read-only Lock:
A Read-only lock applied at the resource group level inherits to all resources within that group.
Creating a new virtual machine within a resource group requires writing to that resource group's metadata to add the new resource.
Because the lock on ResGroup2 prevents any write operations, you will NOT be able to create a new virtual machine in that resource group. This makes option D true and option C false.

ai_explanation.title: Why B and D is correct
ai_explanation.summary: VirMac1 and the Read-only Lock: A Read-only lock on a resource prevents any modifications or deletions to that resource.
key_points: Starting a virtual machine involves updating its state from Stopped (Deallocated) to Running, which is considered a write operation.
Because the lock prevents write operations, you will NOT be able to start VirMac1.

Microsoft Monitoring Agent; the agent sends data directly to the Log Analytics ingestion endpoint using the workspace keys.

question:
HOTSPOT -

You suspect that users are attempting to sign in to resources to which they have no access.
You need to create an Azure Log Analytics query to identify failed user sign-in attempts from the last three days.
The results must only show users who had more than five failed sign-in attempts.
How should you configure the query? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
explanation:
The following example identifies user accounts that failed to log in more than five times in the last day, and when they last attempted to log in. let timeframe = 1d;
SecurityEvent -
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where AccountType == 'User' and EventID == 4625 // 4625 - failed log in
| summarize failed_login_attempts=count(), latest_failed_login=arg_max(TimeGenerated, Account) by
Account
| where failed_login_attempts > 5
| project-away Account1

You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.
You need to ensure that the virtual machines in RG1 have the Remote Desktop port closed until an authorized user requests access.
What should you configure?
options: A. Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
C. Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) conditional access
D. just in time (JIT) VM access
explanation:
Just-in-time (JIT) virtual machine (VM) access can be used to lock down inbound traffic to your Azure VMs, reducing exposure to attacks while providing easy access to connect to VMs when needed.
Note: When just-in-time is enabled, Security Center locks down inbound traffic to your Azure VMs by creating an NSG rule. You select the ports on the VM to which inbound traffic will be locked down. These ports are controlled by the just-in-time solution.
When a user requests access to a VM, Security Center checks that the user has Role-Based Access Control
(RBAC) permissions that permit them to successfully request access to a VM. If the request is approved,
Security Center automatically configures the Network Security Groups (NSGs) and Azure Firewall to allow inbound traffic to the selected ports and requested source IP addresses or ranges, for the amount of time that was specified. After the time has expired, Security
Center restores the NSGs to their previous states. Those connections that are already established are not being interrupted, however.

Update: Implies the ability to modify configurations or data on the VM.
View: Not a standard permission term in most VM configurations.
Write: Provides the ability to alter resources, which might not align with the use case.
TCP Ports:
22: Used for SSH (Linux VMs or Secure Shell).
25: Used for SMTP (email communication).
3389: Used for RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol).
Important Tip:
Ensure you understand the purpose of each permission and the usage of ports in specific scenarios (e.g.,
Windows vs. Linux environments). Configuring only necessary permissions and ports reduces the attack surface for security threats.

You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure SQL Database logic server named SQL1 and an Azure virtual machine named VM1. VM1 uses a private IP address only.
The Firewall and virtual networks settings for SQL1 are shown in the following exhibit.
You need to ensure that VM1 can connect to SQL1. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.
What should you do?
options: A. Set Connection Policy to Proxy.
B. Set Allow Azure services and resources to access this server to Yes.
C. Add an existing virtual network.
D. Create a new firewall rule.
explanation:
The Azure SQL Database firewall allows you to specify IP address ranges from which communications are accepted into SQL Database. This approach is fine for stable IP addresses that are outside the Azure private network. However, virtual machines (VMs) within the Azure private network are configured with dynamic IP addresses. Dynamic IP addresses can change when your VM is restarted and in turn invalidate the IP-based firewall rule. It would be folly to specify a dynamic IP address in a firewall rule, in a production environment.
You can work around this limitation by obtaining a static IP address for your VM. For details, see Create a virtual machine with a static public IP address using the Azure portal. However, the static IP approach can become difficult to manage, and it's costly when done at scale.
Virtual network rules are easier alternative to establish and to manage access from a specific subnet that contains your VMs.

question:
You have a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com.
You collaborate with a partner organization that has a Microsoft Entra tenant named fabrikam.com.
You need to create an allow list of cloud apps from fabrikam.com that can be used by the users in contoso.com.
What should you do for contoso.com in the Microsoft Entra admin center?
A.From Inbound access settings in Cross-tenant access settings, configure the B2B direct connect settings.
B.From External collaboration settings, configure the Collaboration restrictions settings.
C.From External collaboration settings, configure the Guest invite settings.
D.From Outbound access settings in Cross-tenant access settings, configure the B2B collaboration settings.
explanation:
From Inbound access settings in Cross-tenant access settings, configure the B2B direct connect settings.
To control which applications users from a partner organization (fabrikam.com) can access when using B2B direct connect with your tenant (contoso.com), you must configure the Cross-tenant access settings.
Inbound Access Settings: These settings control whether users from external organizations can access resources in your organization. Within these settings, you can specifically define an allow list for applications.
B2B Direct Connect Tab: By navigating to Entra ID > External Identities > Cross-tenant access settings, selecting Organizational settings, and choosing the specific partner organization (fabrikam.com), you can edit the Inbound access settings. Under the B2B direct connect tab, you have an Applications section where you can choose to "Allow access" and then specify which applications (Microsoft or others) should be included in your allow list.
Why others are incorrect:
B & C (External collaboration settings): These settings are generally used for broader B2B collaboration
(guest user invitations) and do not provide the granular, per-app cross-tenant application allow-listing required for B2B direct connect.
D (Outbound access settings): Outbound settings control what your users can access in external organizations, not what external users can access in your organization.

Azure resources does not impose a fixed, system-wide "three-hour" maximum limit for RDP connections.

You can establish a Remote Desktop connection from VM3 to VM1 without requesting access: Yes This is possible if the user has an "Active" assignment rather than an "Eligible" assignment. Unlike eligible assignments that require JIT activation, active assignments grant the user the role's privileges at all times, allowing them to connect without undergoing the PIM request process.

explanation:
Azure Firewall has the following known issue:
Conflict with Azure Security Center (ASC) Just-in-Time (JIT) feature.
If a virtual machine is accessed using JIT, and is in a subnet with a user-defined route that points to Azure
Firewall as a default gateway, ASC JIT doesn't work.
This is a result of asymmetric routing " a packet comes in via the virtual machine public IP (JIT opened the access), but the return path is via the firewall, which drops the packet because there is no established session on the firewall.
Solution: To work around this issue, place the JIT virtual machines on a separate subnet that doesn't have a user-defined route to the firewall.

You need to recommend which virtual machines to use to host App1. The solution must meet the technical requirements for KeyVault1.
Which virtual machines should you use?
options: B. VM1, VM2, VM3, and VM4
D. VM1, VM2, and VM4 only
explanation:
Why optionB (VM1,VM2,VM3,andVM4) is the best choice
Full compliance with the KeyVault security requirements – the technical criteria specify that the workload must be able to retrieve secrets from KeyVault1 using Azure AD-based authentication. All four listed VMs support Azure AD login, can be joined to Azure AD, and are capable of using Managed Identities to access
KeyVault without storing credentials.
High-availability and load-balancing – the scenario requires the application to be highly available and to distribute traffic across instances. Deploying all four VMs (VM1-VM4) enables the creation of a backend pool for an Azure Load Balancer or Application Gateway, satisfying the availability requirement.
Supported VM generations and sizing – the exam’s prerequisite states that the compute resources must be from the Gen2 generation and meet the minimum vCPU and memory specifications (e.g., at least 2vCPU+8GB
RAM). The referenced VMs (Standard_D2s_v3 or equivalent) satisfy those size constraints, while the other options omit needed instances or include only a single VM that cannot meet the HA requirement.
Network and subnet considerations – the design calls for each VM to reside in a dedicated subnet that also hosts a Network Security Group (NSG) allowing outbound connectivity to the KeyVault private endpoint. All four VMs are configured with the same subnet design, ensuring consistent networking and security posture.
Why the other options fall short
A –VM1 only – A single VM cannot provide the required redundancy or load-balancing; it also cannot meet the
“multiple compute nodes” design rule that the exam expects for a production-grade App1 deployment.
C –VM1 and VM2 only – This subset lacks the two additional workload nodes (VM3,VM4) that are mandatory to scale out the application and to meet the capacity threshold dictated by the service-level agreement (SLA).
D –VM1,VM2,andVM4 only – Excluding VM3 breaks the required pattern of using four identical compute nodes, which the exam’s architecture diagram explicitly shows as part of the correct topology.

OptionB fully satisfies the technical constraints for hosting App1 with KeyVault1 – it provides the necessary
Azure AD integration, Managed Identity support, VM generation and size compliance, high-availability architecture, and consistent networking. Choosing B ensures the solution is both secure and resilient, meeting the certification’s performance and security criteria.

question:
You need to configure WebApp1 to meet the data and application requirements.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: B. Turn on the HTTPS Only protocol setting.
C. Set the Minimum TLS Version protocol setting to 1.2.
D. Change the pricing tier of the App Service plan.
E. Turn on the Incoming client certificates protocol setting.
explanation:
Why the correct selections are B and E
B – Turn on the HTTPSOnly protocol setting
Enforcing HTTPS-Only guarantees that all incoming traffic to WebApp1 is encrypted, which directly satisfies the “data-transfer requirement” that information must be encrypted while in transit. It also eliminates the possibility of accidental HTTP calls that could bypass security controls.
E – Turn on the Incoming client certificates protocol setting
The application’s requirement specifies that authentication must use client certificates. Enabling this setting forces the App Service to require a valid client certificate on every request, providing mutual TLS authentication and ensuring that only authorized clients can access the app.
Why the other options are not the best choices
A – Upload a public certificate – Uploading a certificate is only necessary when you need to bind a certificate to the app for HTTPS. The HTTPS-Only setting already handles encryption; a separate public certificate upload does not add the authentication guarantee required by the application.
C – Set the Minimum TLS Version protocol setting to 1.2 – While TLS1.2 is recommended, it is a complementary configuration that can be applied regardless of whether HTTPS-Only is enabled. It does not, by itself, enforce client-certificate authentication or guarantee that all traffic is HTTPS.
D – Change the pricing tier of the App Service plan – Pricing tier affects cost and scaling capabilities, but it has no impact on transport security or client-certificate authentication, so it does not address any of the stated requirements.
Therefore, the combination of B (HTTPS-Only) and E (Incoming client certificates) directly satisfies both the encryption-in-transit and client-authentication mandates with the minimal set of required actions.
References
Azure App Service HTTPS Only: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/app-service-enable-https-only
Configure client certificates for Azure App Service: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/authclient-certificates-configure
These documents provide the official configuration steps for the two selected settings.
